narrator.instruct: Gripping, energetic storyteller telling a true history mystery with a twist, brisk, excited and punchy, never calm.

fleming.instruct: A quiet Scottish scientist in his forties peering at a dish, mildly puzzled and intrigued, dry and understated.

oxford.instruct: A young scientist in a lab bursting with joy at a breakthrough, breathless and thrilled.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before penicillin, an infected scratch could kill you. Then one scientist left a messy bench and went on holiday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: London, nineteen twenty-eight. Alexander Fleming grows the germs that cause boils and blood poisoning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That August he goes on holiday, leaving his germ dishes on the bench, not in the warm incubator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A blue-green mould has landed on one dish. And all around it, the germs are dead.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You see, the mould was making a chemical that kills bacteria. He called it penicillin.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But Fleming couldn't turn it into a usable medicine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Twelve years later, a team at Oxford finally did, in tiny amounts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then American factories scaled it up. By D-Day, there were over two million doses.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now, what if he'd tidied them into the incubator?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One expert argued the germs would have grown first, and the mould would have done nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Maybe someone else finds it, but not in time for the war.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: By some estimates, penicillin and the antibiotics it inspired have saved hundreds of millions of lives.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Maybe someone in your family tree. All thanks to one messy bench.
